## The Polymath Genesis

▶

### The Polymath Nexus

My work lives at the intersection of five disciplines that, in isolation, each shape the world — but together, form a new kind of leverage point for systemic change. I am not a specialist constrained to one lane; I am a synthesist trained to see across lanes simultaneously.

After career disruption and personal loss, I chose to rebuild from scratch rather than simply recover. That decision is not a detour from my story; it is my story.

Employment at the intersection of AI Safety/Security, Finance, and Sustainability — with Accessibility and Humanities as the connective tissue — is what drives me. If technology cannot be designed to help rather than hurt the human experience, then is it worth it? Advocacy and knowledge is why I am here.

I continue to pursue education while actively seeking to balance it with employment and the opportunity to create cutting-edge solutions. As a polymath, I see great opportunities ahead.

View In Practice → [publications.html#recent-papers]

My research investigates failure modes in large language model alignment that emerge not only from model training, but from the interface designs, user populations, and deployment contexts surrounding those models. I am particularly interested in how sycophantic behavior is amplified by UX patterns, how safety guardrails degrade across non-standard communication modalities, and how adversarial prompts exploit intersections of language, culture, and accessibility.

Drawing on empirical expertise in ESG regulatory compliance, enterprise AI deployment at Fortune 500 scale, and community research conducted with the Deaf & DeafBlind Society of Arizona through the PTK Honors in Action program, I bring grounded domain specificity to questions that standard benchmark evaluations do not yet systematically address.

My future research engages with two distinct but complementary areas: sustainability and ESG transparency as they relate to AI compliance and greenwashing risks; and separately, how AI models interact through an HXO lens with accessibility challenges and adoption barriers across disability communities.

On HXO: The most important part of this AI evolution we are living through is the balance between technology and the humans who use it. If technology cannot be designed to help rather than hurt the human experience, then the value proposition collapses. HXO is my frame for ensuring it does not.

I am open to conversations about Fellowships, Cohorts, Grants, Private Executive Mentorships, and collaborative conversations and research programs aligned with these research directions.

## AI Researcher · Builder · Polymath

AAS Sustainable Sciences · BS AI/ML Candidate · PTK Phi Theta Kappa · Nina Mason Pulliam Foundation Scholar

Hello

Thank you for taking a moment to read this. I am Elizabeth Hannan — a non-traditional student, researcher, and polymath in active transition, deliberately upskilling for an adapted future career at the intersection of AI safety, ESG transparency, and human-centered systems design. I bring eighteen-plus years of executive leadership, entrepreneurism, Fortune 500 collaboration, financial communications, and sustainability finance to the academic work I am producing today.

I do not come to this field as an outsider. I come as someone who has led product strategy for Tesla's Supercharger division, directed financial communications at Ellevest (Goldman Sachs), built and scaled companies across IXD, media, and AI enablement, and now applies that lived operational intelligence to research questions that matter: how do AI systems fail, who bears the cost of those failures, and what design principles and governance structures prevent harm at scale?

What I See in a Changing Landscape

The convergence of AI restructuring, ESG regulatory mandates, and economic disruption is not a future event — it is the operating condition of 2026. Organizations that treat AI adoption as a technical deployment problem rather than a human governance challenge will produce systems that are both unsafe and inequitable. I have watched this pattern from the inside of enterprise technology for nearly two decades, and I am building the research foundation to address it directly. My interests extend beyond my formal degrees into public policy and economics — because sustainable AI adoption requires systemic frameworks, not just better models.

HXO Methodology — Human Experience Optimization

I developed and have implemented the HXO (Human Experience Optimization) framework across sixteen years of professional practice. HXO is a design methodology that originates with human outcomes — not with features, technologies, or business requirements — and is grounded in psychology and dimensional spatial intelligence. In an AI adoption context, HXO provides the evaluative lens I apply to every system I research and build: does this help or hurt the full spectrum of human experience? It is not a framework I inherited. It is one I built, tested, and refined across enterprise, startup, and academic contexts.

Mission & Values

What I Stand For

- Open empathy as a design and leadership practice

- Human governance over AI — systems that retain human authority to recalibrate

- Sustainability, ESG, and environmental stewardship as structural commitments

- Accessibility and disability-centered thinking as foundational, not bolted-on

- Service leadership: leading by elevating others, not directing from above

- Long-arc thinking for land, ecosystems, and communities

- Accountability documentation that does not soften uncomfortable findings

After an eon in corporate enterprise tech and entrepreneurism endeavors — it's time to pivot with the most optimal knowledge base in hand and grow. That's why I show up. Every system I research and build is evaluated through one question: does this help or hurt the full spectrum of human experience?

Stranded Capital: Measuring the Economic Cost of AI Accessibility Exclusion Across the Disability Market

This paper introduces the Compounded Exclusion Index (CEI) and Disability-Adjusted Augmentation Rate (DAAR) to measure a structural economic phenomenon in which disabled early-career workers arrive at the labor market precisely as AI augmentation becomes load-bearing for career formation, yet face compounding barriers — a 29-percentage-point postsecondary enrollment gap, platform inaccessibility, and an employment rate less than one-third that of non-disabled peers — creating an adoption cliff from which earnings divergence does not self-correct.

The Adoption Cliff: Early-Career Disabled Workers, AI Skill Formation, and Compounding Economic Exclusion

The Stranded Capital Index™ (SCI), the first formal economic measure of disability market spending power suppressed by AI platform inaccessibility, computed across eight industry sectors to find that e-commerce and financial services carry the highest burden and that AI-driven page complexity is producing a measurable temporal acceleration of market exclusion that regulatory pressure alone is not reversing.

My research investigates failure modes in large language model alignment that emerge not from model training alone, but from the interface designs, user populations, and deployment contexts surrounding those models. A model can be well-aligned in isolation and still behave unsafely in the world — because the world is not a controlled evaluation environment.

That conviction is the throughline of this portfolio.

The technical writing samples here were produced across enterprise AI, data protection, and agentic workflow deployments. Each is structured as an AI system card — the accountability document class that holds an organization publicly responsible for its safety claims. Each contains an explicit disclosure moment: a finding surfaced during documentation review that the engineering or commercial team had not flagged, because the documentation function is itself a safety function.

On HAX: The most important part of this AI evolution we are living through is the balance between technology and the humans who use it. If technology cannot be designed to help rather than hurt the human experience, then the value proposition collapses. HAX is my frame for ensuring it does not.

## System Cards and Technical Writing

Four system card-style technical writing samples produced across enterprise AI deployments in data protection, converged infrastructure, virtualization, and agentic workflow orchestration. Each document applies the accountability architecture of frontier AI safety disclosure — capabilities assessment, adversarial evaluation, known-limitation disclosure, and deployment decision rationale — to production enterprise systems. Findings reflect original documentation engagements; all client identifiers have been adapted under non-disclosure agreements. Select any sample to read in full.

Stranded Capital: Measuring the Economic Cost of AI Accessibility Exclusion Across the Disability Market

This paper introduces the Compounded Exclusion Index (CEI) and Disability-Adjusted Augmentation Rate (DAAR) to measure a structural economic phenomenon in which disabled early-career workers arrive at the labor market precisely as AI augmentation becomes load-bearing for career formation, yet face compounding barriers — a 29-percentage-point postsecondary enrollment gap, platform inaccessibility, and an employment rate less than one-third that of non-disabled peers — creating an adoption cliff from which earnings divergence does not self-correct.

The Stranded Capital Index™ (SCI), the first formal economic measure of disability market spending power suppressed by AI platform inaccessibility, computed across eight industry sectors to find that e-commerce and financial services carry the highest burden and that AI-driven page complexity is producing a measurable temporal acceleration of market exclusion that regulatory pressure alone is not reversing.
